clinicalPearls: A urological emergency in which a retracted foreskin cannot be returned over the glans, forming a constricting band behind the corona
The trapped prepuce and glans become progressively oedematous and painful, and delayed reduction risks arterial compromise, ischaemia, and necrosis of the glans
Commonly iatrogenic, when the foreskin is retracted for catheterisation, cystoscopy, or cleaning and is not replaced afterwards
Prompt manual reduction is the priority - reduce the oedema with sustained compression and adjuncts such as cold or osmotic agents, then push the glans back while drawing the foreskin forward
Adequate analgesia or a penile block greatly aids reduction, and the goal is to relieve the constricting ring as quickly as possible
If manual reduction fails, a dorsal slit or emergency circumcision is performed to release the constriction
Elective circumcision may be offered later to prevent recurrence, and staff should always replace a retracted foreskin after any procedure
reference.pathophysiology: Paraphimosis develops when a tight foreskin is retracted behind the glans and left there. The constricting preputial ring first obstructs venous and lymphatic return from the distal penis, producing progressive oedema of the glans and inner prepuce. This swelling tightens the ring further in a vicious cycle, and if it is not relieved the rising tissue pressure eventually compromises arterial inflow, threatening ischaemia and necrosis of the glans. Management centres on breaking this cycle by reducing the oedema and returning the foreskin to its normal position before irreversible damage occurs.
additionalDifferentials: Preputial or penile oedema from another cause, such as insect bite or allergic angio-oedema
Penile tourniquet syndrome from an encircling hair or thread
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis by inspection of the retracted foreskin and constricting ring
Assessment of glans colour and capillary refill to gauge perfusion
Blood glucose, given the association of recurrent balanoposthitis with diabetes
Swab if secondary infection is suspected
Review of recent instrumentation or catheter history
redFlags: A dusky, dark, or blistering glans indicating ischaemia
Absent capillary refill of the glans
Signs of necrosis or systemic sepsis
reference.prognosis: Excellent when reduced promptly; the outlook worsens sharply with delay, when tissue ischaemia and glans necrosis can occur, so time to reduction is critical.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise it as an emergency and delaying reduction
Retracting a foreskin for catheterisation or examination and forgetting to replace it, the commonest iatrogenic cause
Attempting reduction without adequate analgesia and without first reducing the oedema
Confusing paraphimosis (foreskin stuck retracted) with phimosis (foreskin that cannot be retracted)
Missing early ischaemic changes of the glans
management: Perform prompt manual reduction as first-line: reduce glans oedema with sustained circumferential compression, then advance the foreskin back over the glans
Provide adequate analgesia or a penile dorsal-nerve block to facilitate reduction
Use adjuncts to shrink the oedema before reduction, such as cold compression, osmotic agents (granulated sugar) or a wrapped elastic compression bandage
If manual reduction fails, escalate urgently to a dorsal slit incision to release the constricting ring, or emergency circumcision
Assess glans perfusion by colour and capillary refill throughout, as delay risks ischaemia and necrosis of the glans
Prevent recurrence by always replacing the foreskin after catheterisation, cystoscopy or cleaning, and offer elective circumcision for recurrent episodes or significant phimosis
Screen for and manage predisposing factors such as diabetes and recurrent balanoposthitis
